title: Kernel Interaction Correlation Lab and Investigation Checklist
author: Priya Nair
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines a repeatable lab and step-by-step investigation checklist for diagnosing subtle kernel-level interaction issues in the serving runtime (contention, preemption races, KV cache coherence artifacts, and cross-kernel priority inversion). The intent is to provide a reproducible experimental harness, required telemetry fields, and a prioritized checklist on-call and SRE engineers can follow.

Audience: runtime SREs, performance engineers, kernel engineers, and on-call rotation members.

Scope and when to use this guide
- Use this playbook when: tail latency spikes (>99th percentile increases by >2x), unexplained GPU scheduler stalls, intermittent model-switch oscillations, or when a regression appears only under mixed-concurrency workloads.
- Out of scope: hardware-level power faults (use hardware incident runbook), application-level correctness bugs in the model code.

Background and rationale
- Modern inference workloads combine continuous batching, KV cache, and multiple kernel variants. Subtle interactions (e.g., a long-running kernel holding a tensor memory lock while preemption is attempted) can manifest as short-lived but high-impact latency spikes. These interactions are difficult to identify from high-level traces; causal correlation across runtime, kernel scheduler, and GPU dispatch telemetry is required.

Telemetry and signal catalog (required)
- Request-level signals:
  - request_id (string)
  - route/model (string)
  - timestamp_queued_ms (int)
  - timestamp_kernel_enqueue_ms (int)
  - timestamp_kernel_start_ms (int)
  - timestamp_kernel_end_ms (int)
  - cpu_thread (string)
  - kernel_variant (string)
  - batch_id (string)
  - kv_cache_hit_ratio (float)
  - tokens_generated (int)

- Kernel/dispatcher signals:
  - gpu_dispatch_time_ms
  - gpu_complete_time_ms
  - kernel_preempt_attempts (int)
  - kernel_preempt_duration_ms
  - occupancy_percent
  - tensor_memory_alloc_bytes
  - kernel_wait_queue_len

- System signals:
  - node_cpu_load_1m
  - node_gpu_temp_celsius
  - nvlink_retry_count
  - iommu_faults
  - cgroup_preempt_events

Quick reference thresholds (operational defaults)
- 99th percentile latency increase: alert if > 2x baseline for 5m window.
- Kernel preempt attempts: alert if > 10 attempts/min on a node.
- GPU occupancy: alert if > 95% for sustained 2m while tail latency increases.

Investigation checklist (ordered, prescriptive)
1) Triage and collect artifacts (first 10 minutes)
   - Capture high-level traces: request traces for the afflicted timeframe (trace ID or request_id).
   - Export kernel-level telemetry: gpu_dispatch_time_ms, kernel_variant per batch, preempt counters.
   - Snapshot node-level metrics: top process GPU memory, nvtop snapshot, nvidia-smi dmon 1s for 30s.
   - Preserve scheduler logs and admission controller decision logs for the period.

2) Fast correlation (10–30 minutes)
   - Correlate request trace timestamps with kernel start/end timestamps. Look for requests with long gap between kernel_enqueue and kernel_start (queueing at CPU/dispatcher).
   - Identify whether affected requests share model/version or batch shape. If yes, candidate a model-specific kernel variant.
   - Query: Prometheus example
     - promql: |
       increase(kernel_preempt_attempts_total[5m])
       
   - Quick grep on dispatcher logs for spike patterns: grep -E "preempt|handoff|wait_queue" /var/log/runtime/dispatcher.log | sed -n '1,200p'

3) Kernel-level deep-dive (30–120 minutes)\   - Reconstruct kernel timeline using kernel_trace_id map to request_ids.
   - If preemption attempts are present, examine preempt_duration_ms distribution. Long durations indicate stalled preempt handlers or unexpected GPU stall.
   - Run a focused microbenchmark: replay a small synthetic trace containing the same batch sizes and sequence lengths. Use the lab harness described below.

4) Hypothesis-driven fault injection (1–3 hours)
   - Hypothesis examples:
     - H1: A kernel variant with large scratch memory occasionally triggers a slow tensor allocation path causing long preempt durations.
     - H2: KV cache hot-skip path causes serialization on a shared mutex while kernel handoff waits, causing queue buildup.
   - For H1: deploy a canary variant with reduced scratch growth (quantized variant) and run shadow traffic. Observe preempt and tail latency.
   - For H2: run mutex contention stress test: deliberately increase concurrent KV hits on same keyspace and observe kernel_wait_queue_len.

5) Mitigation and rollback (if confirmed)
   - Immediate mitigations:
     - Route affected traffic to fallback kernel variant or smaller model variant.
     - Temporarily reduce max_concurrency for the node to shed potential long-running kernels.
   - Rollback checklist:
     - Validate fallback route maintains 95th/99th latency SLOs for a 10-minute observation window.
     - If stable, start a staged rollout of the stable kernel variant with 10/30/60 minute ramp steps.

Lab experiment protocol (reproducible)
- Goal: reproduce tail-latency spike deterministically in the lab, isolate kernel interaction sequence, and test mitigations.

Prerequisites:
- Lab cluster with identical GPU family and runtime build (container image tag).
- Corpus of requests: select real traffic sample (anonymized) with 1k requests covering observed sequence length distribution.
- Harness repo: git@internal:redwood/runtime-labs.git, branch: telemetry-repro-2024

Steps:
1. Environment setup\   - Deploy runtime image: docker run --rm -e RUNTIME_TAG=telemetry-repro-2024 redwood/runtime:telemetry-repro-2024\   - Ensure profiling sidecar enabled (ENV: ENABLE_PROFILE=1) and lightweight BPF tracing agent running (rbpf-agent).
2. Load injection\   - Use lab injector: ./injector --corpus=corpus/sample-telemetry-corpus.json --qps=target --concurrency=target --shape=traffic-shape.yaml --trace-prefix=test-repro\   - Example: ./injector --corpus=sample.json --qps=120 --concurrency=64 --shape=mixed-burst.yaml --trace-prefix=test-repro
3. Collect artifacts automatically\   - run: ./collect-artifacts --since "2024-07-15T00:00:00Z" --out ./artifacts/test-repro.tar.gz\   - Artifacts: traces/*.json, kernel_telemetry.csv, dispatcher.log, nvidia-dmon.log, rbpf-traces/*.perf
4. Repeatability notes\   - Run at least 5 iterations per configuration; seed injector with deterministic random seed.

Observability playbook: queries and examples\- Prometheus examples:
  - Tail latency spike detection (5m): |
    (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)))
  - Kernel preempt heatmap: |
    sum by (node, kernel_variant) (increase(kernel_preempt_attempts_total[15m]))

- Trace join example (SQL-ish pseudocode for internal trace store): |
  SELECT r.request_id, r.route, t.kernel_variant, t.start_ms, t.end_ms
  FROM requests r JOIN kernel_spans t ON r.trace_id = t.trace_id
  WHERE r.timestamp BETWEEN '2024-07-15T10:00:00Z' AND '2024-07-15T10:10:00Z'
  ORDER BY t.start_ms DESC

Kernel-level capture snippets
- BPF tracer snippet (example): |
  sudo rbpf-agent --attach=nv_dispatch --out /tmp/rbpf-attach.log --fields pid,tgid,dispatch_timestamp,kernel_name,stack_id

- nvidia-smi sampling (30s high-fidelity window): |
  nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1000 -o TD > nvidia-dmon.log &

- Minimal script to extract slow kernel spans (bash): |
  awk -F',' '$6 - $5 > 50 {print $0}' kernel_telemetry.csv | head -n 200

Fault injection template (Caution: only run in lab or staging)
- Introduce artificial allocation latency at the runtime allocator path to emulate slow scratch growth:
  - Use LD_PRELOAD wrapper which sleeps on gpu_alloc path once every N allocations.
  - Invocation YAML snippet: |
    fault_injection:
      type: allocator-sleep
      sleep_ms: 25
      every_n: 1000

Acceptance criteria for mitigations
- Measured improvement: 99th latency returns to within 1.2x baseline and kernel_preempt_attempts drop by >= 60% in 15-minute window.
- No increase in error rate or model output degradation (compare eval prompts used in shadow traffic).

Runbook ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: runtime-sre@redwood.com (rotation: oncall-runtime).
- Secondary: kernel-team@redwood.com.
- Pager escalation: if mitigation not effective within 30 minutes, escalate to oncall-eng-lead and open a Sev-2 incident.

Post-incident hygiene
1. Tag all artifacts and traces with incident id: INC-YYYYMMDD-XXX.
2. Record principal hypothesis and final resolution in the incident doc.
3. Add a regression test to the microbenchmark suite (benchmarks/interaction-regressions) if the issue was root-caused to a kernel variant.

Appendix: example artifact file formats
- kernel_telemetry.csv (columns): timestamp_ms, node, gpu_id, batch_id, kernel_variant, start_ms, end_ms, preempt_attempts, preempt_duration_ms, tensor_alloc_bytes
- dispatcher.log entries: timestamp iso8601 | node | event | details

Appendix: common failure patterns (cheat sheet)
- Pattern: "enqueue drift" — long gap between kernel_enqueue and kernel_start; likely dispatcher saturation or priority inversion.
- Pattern: "preempt tail" — repeated preempt attempts with long preempt_duration_ms; likely kernel stall or driver-level hang.
- Pattern: "kv hotlock" — KV cache hit correlation with dispatcher mutex contention; look for high kv_cache_hit_ratio and mutex wait traces.

Related pages and artifacts
- Add links to the final artifacts tarball in the incident doc and tag the change with the runtime build that was running.

Maintenance and cadence
- This playbook is reviewed quarterly by the profiling team. Add new signal fields when the runtime or kernel telemetry schema changes.

Contact and feedback
- For clarifications or to propose changes to the checklist, open a pull request against runtime-labs/docs/kernel-interaction-checklist.md or ping Priya Nair on Slack (#runtime-profiling).

End of document
